Kolno Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Kolno, Poland

Not demolished. Kolno's Jewish settlement developed from the end of the 18th century, reaching 2,216 people (49 percent of the town) by 1921; earlier, Kolno's Jews had been buried in Śniadowo and Łomża, until this cemetery was established following an 1817 government decision requiring annual rent payment. After the German army conquered the town in summer 1941, a pogrom broke out involving some local Poles, and Jews were later forced to leave town and were shot in the forest near Mściwuje. During the summer 1941 antisemitic violence, Jews were also forced to bury a statue of Lenin in this cemetery, which was also used for executions. In 2005, at the initiative of Rabbi Shlomo Besser, the family of Emanuel Toporowitz of Kolno, and the Foundation for the Preservation of Jewish Heritage in Poland, the cemetery was cleaned and refenced.
